strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Presence is replacing permanent residence, Knight Frank finds, as 129 people a day cross the USD 30 million line and London becomes a city to dip in and out of
lead.standfirst: Knight Frank's reading of the prime property market describes owners who hold many addresses and live fully in none, with direct consequences for the people who run them.
lead.body:
Global luxury residential prices rose 3.2 per cent in 2025, Knight Frank reports in its analysis of the Wealth Report 2026, extending a run that began in early 2023 and that has outpaced mainstream house prices. Of the 100 markets tracked by its Prime International Residential Index, 73 recorded gains. Behind the headline lies a more interesting shift in behaviour. Liam Bailey's colleague Andrew Pritchard puts it plainly: "presence is rapidly replacing permanent residence" among the most mobile buyers.

The divergence between cities shows what that means in practice. London prime values fell 4.7 per cent, yet super-prime rents there have risen 53 per cent over five years, and close to half of prime central London purchases are made without a mortgage. Knight Frank calls the capital the ultimate "dip-in, dip-out" city: a place families use for a season, a school term or a set of meetings, and rent or hold lightly. Paris rose 1.3 per cent. In Italy a EUR 300,000 flat-tax regime has produced deep shortages in Milan and is pushing buyers towards Rome and Lake Como. In New York prices rose 0.8 per cent but turnkey stock is scarce, and the Upper East Side is recording record transaction speeds. Miami absorbed about USD 3 billion of super-prime sales, with South Beach ultra-prime above USD 5,000 per square foot.

Asia tells a similar story with different numbers. The region averaged 3.6 per cent growth. Singapore rose 7.9 per cent and climbed from fifth to fourth on the index, despite a 60 per cent Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty that constrains volumes. Hong Kong fell 2.1 per cent but still recorded 81 transactions of USD 10 million or more in the fourth quarter, second only to Dubai.

The demand beneath all this is growing quickly. Knight Frank expects about 129 people a day to cross the USD 30 million wealth threshold over the next five years. Many will buy, rent or borrow several homes at once, in different tax and legal systems, and expect each to be ready on the day they arrive.
lead.why: A family with five addresses and no fixed home needs a house manager who can run continuity: staff, stock, security and paperwork that follow the principal from city to city. The estate is no longer one building but a network, and the person who keeps it coherent is the product.

articles.title: The world's ultra-wealthy population grew 14.4 per cent in 2025 to a record 556,850, Altrata finds, and will near 750,000 by 2030
articles.body:
Altrata's World Ultra Wealth Report 2026, published in June, counts 556,850 people with a net worth above USD 30 million, the strongest annual expansion since 2017 at 14.4 per cent. In two years the group has grown by almost 30 per cent, adding more than 120,000 people. Together they hold USD 63.8 trillion, more than twice the annual output of the United States, of which about USD 26 trillion is investable.

The geography is changing. North America adds the largest absolute number, about 77,000 more by 2030, taking it above 300,000 people, and roughly four in five of its ultra-wealthy are self-made. Asia grew 15.8 per cent in 2025 and has the strongest forecast growth of the three major regions, led by India, China, the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia. Altrata projects a global population of 746,570 and combined wealth of USD 85 trillion by 2030.

Two details matter for anyone who will serve these families. Women make up 12 per cent of the group today and Altrata expects 19 per cent by 2040. And purely inherited wealth accounts for only 6 per cent of the total, which means most of the households now entering the market built their fortunes recently and are assembling their first serious domestic organisation, rather than inheriting one.
articles.why: New money without a household tradition hires on trust and learns on the job. The manager who can explain how a well-run house operates, and set it up without condescension, is worth far more to such a principal than one who only follows inherited routine.

articles.title: North American business aviation rose 0.9 per cent in September, beating a forecast decline, as large-cabin fractional flying jumped 13.9 per cent
articles.body:
Argus International reported on 8 October that North American business aviation activity rose 0.9 per cent in September. The result defied expectations: the same analyst had projected, in its August review, a 0.1 per cent decline that would have been the first negative year-on-year month of 2026. The large-cabin fractional segment led, up 13.9 per cent.

The August figures show where the growth comes from. Overall activity rose only 0.3 per cent, well below a 3.5 per cent forecast, yet fractional flying was up 7.9 per cent, with large-cabin fractional up 14.9 per cent. Charter (Part 135) was flat at plus 0.1 per cent, while owner-operated flying under Part 91 fell 2.9 per cent, with midsize and large-cabin aircraft down more than 13 per cent. Argus analyst Travis Kuhn called August a seasonal transition month and said the market remained healthy.

The pattern is consistent: families are still flying, but fewer of them are flying aircraft they own and operate. Shares, cards and managed programmes are absorbing the demand, and with them the logistics of scheduling, catering, ground handling and crew coordination move from a flight department to a service contract.
articles.why: A concierge increasingly books capacity rather than directing a tail number. Knowing how fractional, card and charter products differ, and what each demands in notice, catering and customs planning, is now a core travel skill.

articles.title: Average tenure in private service has fallen from about 20 years to about three, and a butler now lasts 2.6 years, Morgan & Mallet reports
articles.body:
The Morgan & Mallet Household Staff Industry Report 2026 draws on the agency's own placement data, which it cautions is self-reported rather than independent research. Its headline is a collapse in tenure: from about 20 years in the traditional model to roughly three today. By role, a butler averages 2.6 years, a chauffeur 3.8 years and a housekeeper 4.0 years. The domestic couple, historically the anchor of a house, lasts longest at 4.2 years.

Pay explains part of the churn. Private chefs are placed at up to USD 300,000 in the United States, estate managers up to USD 250,000, butlers and nannies between USD 90,000 and USD 180,000, housekeepers USD 80,000 to USD 160,000 and chauffeurs USD 80,000 to USD 130,000. The United States and Switzerland together account for nearly nine in ten of the highest-paying roles placed. Estate managers draw about 80 applications per search and bring about 17 years of experience on average, making them the third most contested role; personal assistants attract about 112 per search.

The hardest posts to fill are not the best paid. Domestic couples draw about 24 applications per search, and 21 per cent of French clients report being unable to fill the role. In France, the net monthly cost of a couple has roughly doubled in a decade. Retention can be built: 91 per cent of New York private chef placements complete their full annual contract.
articles.why: If a three-year stay is now normal, the manager's real task is continuity: written household standards, handover files and a bench of trusted people, so that the house does not reset each time someone leaves.

briefs.t: A flat tax is draining Milan
briefs.b: Italy's EUR 300,000 flat-tax regime for new residents has created deep supply shortages in Milan and is pushing buyers towards Rome and Lake Como, Knight Frank reports. Families relocating on that scheme tend to need a house set up quickly, from staff to security.

briefs.t: Women are 12 per cent of the ultra-wealthy
briefs.b: Altrata counts women as 12 per cent of the world's ultra-high-net-worth population and expects 19 per cent by 2040. Principals are changing, and so are their expectations of household and family-office service.

Owner-operated flying fell 2.9 per cent in August in North America while fractional rose 7.9 per cent, Argus data reported by Private Jet Card Comparisons show. Midsize and large-cabin Part 91 flights were each down more than 13 per cent.
